holes_found.description: Citation precision: 'Doodson 1921, Table II' is cited as the source for the explicit '(7/2)·e' coefficient. Doodson's Table II provides expansion coefficients in his own argument-number notation; the compact '(7/2)·e' formulation is the modern textbook presentation (e.g., Pugh, Sea-Level Science, 2014; Cartwright, Tides: A Scientific History, 1999) derived from Doodson's expansion. A reader pulling Doodson 1921 to verify '(7/2)·e' verbatim will not find that exact form in the table. The math is correct and Doodson is the canonical primary source for the underlying expansion, so this is a precision issue, not a factual error.
holes_found.recommendation: Either (a) add a parenthetical co-citation to a modern textbook (e.g., Pugh 2014 §5.3, or Cartwright 1999) immediately after the existing Doodson link, or (b) leave Doodson as the deep-source citation and reword to 'as developed in Doodson 1921 and standardly presented as N2/M2 ≈ (7/2)·e in modern texts.' Either preserves the historical primary citation while telling the reader where (7/2)·e is actually written in that exact form.

holes_found.description: Rounding sensitivity in 'back-solves to e ≈ 0.054 ... to better than 1%'. Using the rounded N2/M2 ≈ 0.19 as given in the same sentence: e = (2/7)(0.19) = 0.0543, vs. measured 0.0549 → ~1.1% off (not 'better than 1%'). Using more precise Cartwright-Tayler-Edden ratio N2/M2 ≈ 0.1914: e = 0.0547 → 0.36% off, which IS 'better than 1%'. The claim is therefore internally tight if a slightly more precise ratio is used upstream, but as written the chain 0.19 → 0.054 → 1% is marginally inconsistent.
holes_found.recommendation: Trivial fix: write the back-solve as 'N2/M2 ≈ 0.191 back-solves to e ≈ 0.0546' (or 0.0547), preserving the 'better than 1%' claim with mathematically consistent precision. Alternatively drop the '<1%' qualifier and say 'matching the measured lunar eccentricity e ≈ 0.0549 to within a few percent.'

stronger_arguments.description: When refuting the gear-motion defender (analyst's pending EXP-2789): the cleanest empirical answer is that the N2/M2 ratio is observationally stable across decadal-scale tide gauge records globally, with phase relationships consistent with Keplerian elliptic motion. A gear-driven angular-velocity function tuned to reproduce N2/M2 = 0.19 would also have to reproduce the relative PHASE of N2 vs M2 at every coastal station — an over-constrained problem with no published dome solution.
sources: Pugh & Woodworth, 'Sea-Level Science', Cambridge UP, 2014, Tables 5.2 / 5.3 (constituent amplitudes and phases)

kernel_of_truth.description: The dome author's instinct that N2 'arises from the lunar elliptic circuit' is structurally on the right track: the standard tidal-theory derivation does run through Keplerian elliptic motion, and the lunar eccentricity is the physical input that generates N2 against the M2 baseline. The patch this run actually strengthens this charitable reading by making the standard-physics derivation explicit and quantitative ((7/2)·e gives e ≈ 0.054 vs measured 0.0549 — Wikipedia-grade derivation, not a strawman).
kernel_of_truth.why_it_doesnt_save_claim: Knowing 'N2 needs eccentricity' is necessary but not sufficient — the dome model has to PRODUCE an eccentricity from its own parameters. Cited fields confirm the gap: data/wins.json:WIN-051.detail_evidence states the dome has 'never (1) specified an orbital eccentricity for this moon, (2) derived one from dome geometry, or (3) calculated N2's amplitude or its ratio to M2 from dome parameters'; raw-text/monitor.py contains no N2 domain; raw-text/formulas.json has no entry. The kernel-of-truth is 'the standard physics is correct'; the WIN is claimed under a dome verdict, so the standard physics being correct refutes rather than rescues the dome claim.

deeper_analysis: The ISS-2788 patch was the load-bearing fix on this WIN. Before the patch the math was an inferior approximation that back-solved to e ≈ 0.063 — embarrassingly off from measured 0.0549 by ~15%, and trivially attackable as 'critical review uses wrong coefficient'. After the patch the math is textbook-tight and the verdict carries more weight: N2/M2 ≈ (7/2)·e, observed 0.19 → e ≈ 0.054 — within a percent of measured. The 'Self-Contradicted' verdict is now well-supported because the standard-physics derivation is precisely the derivation the dome model has to supply and cannot. Three remaining minor findings (Doodson citation precision, rounding sensitivity in the '<1%' claim, double-hyperlink cosmetics) are tractable single-sentence edits — none of them undermines the argument or invites a verdict change.
